prime.problem: A model stored at 16 bits per weight is slow to generate with and may not even fit in memory. Dropping bits makes it smaller and faster, but past a point the answers get worse, and a suspiciously fast host may be doing exactly that without saying so.
prime.fits: Third mechanism card: the bytes side of the memory-bandwidth division. Hardware raised the bandwidth; quantization shrinks what has to be read per token. MoE, next, shrinks it a different way.
prime.goal: Choose a quantization level for a use case, and predict roughly what it does to size, speed and quality.

attend: Why does 3.3× smaller give only 2.47× faster, not 3.3×?
Why does going from 4-bit (Q4_K_M) to 2-bit (Q2_K) buy only 11% more speed while quality drops noticeably?
Why does quantization do little for a slow first token on a long prompt?
Why is perplexity a poor guide to damage on code and math?

must: Fewer bits per weight → fewer bytes read per token → decode is bandwidth-bound → tokens come faster (F16 → Q4_K_M: 29.17 → 71.93 t/s)
Packed weights must be unpacked before use → extra compute per byte → speed rises less than size falls → gains shrink below about 4 bits while quality loss grows
Quantization only speeds the memory-bound writing phase → prefill is compute-bound → a long-prompt TTFT barely changes → use caching there instead
elevated: Hosts choose precision for you → OpenRouter lists bf16 / fp8 / fp4 per provider → a fast or cheap host may be fp4 → compare speeds only at the same precision

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–4 sentences why dropping bits speeds up generation, why the speed-up is less than the size reduction, and where the sweet spot is. Add one sentence on what quantization does not speed up.
checklist: fewer bytes per token → faster in a bandwidth-bound decode
dequantization compute means speed-up < size reduction
sweet spot 4–8 bits: most of the speed for <1% perplexity at 5–8 bits
below ~4 bits: small speed gain, noticeable quality loss

retrieve.q: Explain why Ollama ships Q4_K_M by default rather than F16 or Q2_K.
answer: F16 is 3.3× bigger and about 2.5× slower, and may not fit
Q2_K is only ~11% faster than Q4_K_M with noticeably worse output
Q4_K_M gets most of the speed at a small quality cost

retrieve.q: Walk through what changes, step by step, when the same Llama-3.1-8B goes from Q8_0 to Q4_K_M: bytes per token, predicted speed, measured speed.
answer: size 7.95 → 4.58 GiB: about 1.7× fewer bytes per token
a pure bandwidth model predicts about 1.7× faster
measured 50.93 → 71.93 t/s ≈ 1.41×: dequantization eats part of the gain

retrieve.q: You're generating SQL for a production database on a hosted open model. Two hosts: one fp4 at 2× the speed, one bf16. Which do you pick and what would change your mind?
answer: prefer bf16 (or fp8): precise tasks suffer more than perplexity shows
switch to fp4 only if you measure your own task quality and it holds
or if answers are checked cheaply, so a rare error costs a retry

compare.q: Quantization and MoE both cut the bytes read per token. Which one also cuts the memory needed to hold the model, and which cuts bytes by more?
answer: quantization shrinks both storage and bytes read (about 4× from 16 to 4 bits)
MoE cuts bytes read by 9–23× but you still hold every expert
they combine: MoE models are usually also quantized

compare.q: On a laptop, quantization is about fitting and single-user speed. What changes when a server quantizes for many users, and why can weight-only quantization help less there?
answer: servers batch many users, so each weight read serves many tokens
at high batch the step is less bandwidth-bound, so fewer weight bytes help less
servers then also quantize activations or the KV cache, and care about throughput per GPU

predict.q: You move from Q4_K_M to Q8_0 on the M3 to get better code. Predict the new speed for qwen3.5:4b from the measured 15.4 t/s, using the card's Llama ratio, and say whether you'd notice it on an 82-token answer.
predict.answer: The Llama table gives 71.93 → 50.93 t/s, about 0.71×, so roughly 15.4 × 0.71 ≈ 10.9 t/s. An 82-token answer goes from about 5.3 s to about 7.5 s of writing: noticeable, but small next to the 653-token vs 82-token difference. Worth it if the code gets better.

apply.task: Pull two quantizations of the same small model in Ollama (for example a Q4_K_M and a Q8_0 tag). For each, record the size on disk, the eval rate on the same ~300-token prompt, and judge the output on three tasks where precision matters (a regex, a SQL query, a unit conversion).
apply.done: You have size, speed and a quality verdict for both, and the speed ratio is below the size ratio (dequantization overhead). You've decided which you'll keep for which task.
apply.hint: Ollama tags like :q8_0 and :q4_K_M exist for many models; ollama list shows sizes.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how much speed you give up at 8 bits?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why speed rises less than size falls?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: bits → bytes per token, or bits → quality?
Which of your tasks is precise enough that you should avoid 4-bit or fp4?
What do you expect MoE to do that quantization can't?
